prompt: What makes a test flaky, in the sense this lesson uses?

choices.text: It fails on every run until somebody fixes the page
choices.why: That is lesson 3's search defect at a robot's speed: a defect, and a test doing its job.

choices.text: Its verdict varies on the same code
choices.why: Right. Same shop, same test, same machine, and one run green while the next is red.

choices.text: It is slow
choices.why: A slow test that always gives the same verdict is slow, not flaky; the failing gate runs were slower because a check waited out its time.

choices.text: It was written without web-first assertions
choices.why: Those help with one cause, timing; the shared basket breaks tests that use them throughout.

prompt: Why does the lesson call a test that fails five runs in ten worse than one that fails every run?

choices.text: It hides more defects in the page
choices.why: The page is the same in both cases; what differs is what the red teaches the people who see it.

choices.text: Every failing run costs more machine time than a passing one
choices.why: The failing runs were slower, but the lesson's argument is about people, not seconds.

choices.text: People learn to re-run it, even a real red
choices.why: Right. A red that goes away on a second run means *try again*, and the day it is real it is read the same way.

choices.text: Playwright refuses to report it
choices.why: Playwright reports every failure; with retries it even names the flaky ones.

prompt: Match each case from the platform's history to its cause.

pairs.left: A course card read before the screen was redrawn
Two test packages inserting the school `code` at once
`vim` returning to the line held in an earlier screenshot
Fonts that one machine could fetch and the other could not

prompt: `ssr.spec.js` and `waiting.spec.js`, ten times each, give 20 passed with `--workers 1` and 3 failed with `--workers 2`, each receiving a count of 2. Which cause is that?

choices.text: Order: one ran before the other
choices.why: With one worker they also ran one after another, twenty times, and every run passed; both reset first.

choices.text: Timing: the page was slower with two workers
choices.why: A slow page would make the count late, not 2; the 2 is a mango the ssr test never added.

choices.text: Shared state: one basket, two tests at the same moment
choices.why: Right. Passing alone and failing together, with a value that is another test's work, is its signature.

choices.text: Environment: the second worker had a different browser
choices.why: Both workers start the same Chromium 141 from the same configuration.

prompt: The platform keeps a test that fails roughly once in a million runs, when the code `000000` happens to be right. Why does the lesson treat that differently from the gate's flaky pair?

choices.text: Its rate was worked out and written beside it
choices.why: Right. A known, stated rate of one in a million is a decision; five in ten that nobody measured is a problem.

choices.text: Go tests are not allowed to be flaky, so it cannot count
choices.why: Nothing makes a Go test immune; the comment beside it admits the flake and gives its odds.

choices.text: It only fails on the build machine
choices.why: The odds are the same on every machine; it is not an environment case.

choices.text: Because a second-factor test is retried automatically
choices.why: No retry is involved; a retry would hide the rate instead of stating it.

prompt: A screen shows a defect only when its content is shuffled one particular way, about one run in three. A colleague adds retries so the suite stops failing. What has happened?

choices.text: The flake is gone, because the shuffle now settles
choices.why: A retry changes nothing about the shuffle; it gives the test two more draws to miss the defect.

choices.text: A real defect now passes nearly every run
choices.why: Right. Here the flake was the defect showing; the platform fixed its own case by asking for each outcome by name.

choices.text: The test now checks both outcomes
choices.why: It checks whichever outcome each attempt happens to draw, and passes on the first good draw.

choices.text: Nothing, retries only affect the order of tests
choices.why: Retries rerun a failed test; they change the verdict the suite reports.

prompt: Put the diagnosis of a flaky test in order.
items: Run it many times with `--repeat-each` and count the failures
Change one condition, such as `--workers`, and count again
Read the trace kept from a failing attempt
Fix the cause, then count again where it failed most
trap: Reading one red run closely before counting turns a sample of one into a story.

prompt: The typing test failed 5 of 20 with two workers and 6 of 20 with one. The ssr and waiting pair failed 0 times with one worker and 3 with two. What does that contrast tell you?

choices.text: Both are shared state, since both were run with `--workers`
choices.why: Running with the flag proves nothing; what matters is whether the rate moved, and for the typing test it barely did.

choices.text: The pair shares data; the typing test's cause is inside it
choices.why: Right. A rate that jumps with workers says sharing, and the count of 2 names what was shared; a rate that stays put points at the test and its page.

choices.text: Nothing: twenty runs are too few to compare anything
choices.why: Twenty is few for proving a rare failure gone, but 0 against 3 beside 5 against 6 is a pattern worth reading.

choices.text: Two workers make the machine too slow for both
choices.why: Then the typing test would have moved too; it failed slightly more with one worker, not with two.

prompt: In the two `race.mjs` runs at 145 ms a key, what decided whether the list ended on one fruit or three?

choices.text: How long the test waited before reading
choices.why: Both runs waited for `aria-busy="false"`; the list was already final when it was read.

choices.text: Which answer landed last
choices.why: Right. In one run the answer to `pap` was drawn last; in the other, the answer to `pa`, at 815 ms.

choices.text: How fast the keys were typed
choices.why: Both runs typed at 145 ms a key, and the questions left about 150 ms apart in both.

choices.text: Whether the server answered `p` at all
choices.why: It answered all six questions in both runs; only the order of arrival differed.

prompt: With `--retries 2`, a test fails its first attempt and passes the second. How does Playwright count it?

choices.text: Passed
choices.why: It is not counted with the tests that passed first time; that is what the third verdict is for.

choices.text: Failed
choices.why: The run counts it as having come through; a failure is a test that failed every attempt.

choices.text: Flaky
choices.why: Right. The summary prints the count, as in *7 flaky* on the quarantined test.

choices.text: Skipped, because the retry replaced it
choices.why: It ran every attempt; skipped is for a test that did not run at all.

prompt: The shared-basket pair, with `--retries 2`, prints *5 flaky, 15 passed* and exits with code 0. What did the retries hide?

choices.text: Nothing: the failures were noise
choices.why: They were two tests seeing each other's fruit, a defect in how the suite shares data.

choices.text: That the page shows a wrong count
choices.why: The page counted correctly what was in the basket; the defect is in the tests sharing it.

choices.text: A server that was slow to answer under load
choices.why: The failures received 2 instead of 1, which no amount of waiting explains.

choices.text: A defect in the suite, behind an open gate
choices.why: Right. Exit code 0 opens the gate, and the only trace of the shared basket is one line nobody reads on a green build.

prompt: Complete the command so that retries still run but any test that needed one makes the run exit with an error: `npx playwright test --retries 2 --___`
This project puts its quarantined test in a folder the default configuration does not read, rather than relying only on a tag and `--grep-invert`. Why?

choices.text: Tags do not work with the list reporter
choices.why: Tags work with every reporter; the test carries one as well.

choices.text: The plain command is the gate
choices.why: Right. A tag keeps a test out only of the runs that remember `--grep-invert`; a folder cannot be forgotten.

choices.text: A folder makes the test pass
choices.why: The quarantine job above still failed eight attempts in twenty; the folder only changes which run decides.

choices.text: Playwright forbids two test folders in one configuration
choices.why: The point is the opposite: each configuration reads its own folder on purpose.

prompt: Match each way of handling a known problem to what it says.

pairs.right: Does not apply here; not run
Broken, to be fixed; not run
Fails every time; a pass is an error
Fails some of the time; runs apart from the gate

prompt: `test.fail()` is added to the 145 ms typing test and it runs twenty times. The search defect shows on 7 of the attempts. What does the summary say?

choices.text: 20 passed, because the annotation covers the test
choices.why: The annotation expects a failure, and every attempt where the page behaved is a pass under it, which is an error.

choices.text: 7 failed, 13 passed
choices.why: That reads the attempts as if there were no annotation; under `test.fail()` the seven that met the defect are the ones that pass.

choices.text: 13 failed, 7 passed
choices.why: Right. Each of the thirteen says *Expected to fail, but passed*: an annotation for *always fails* cannot describe a test that fails some of the time.

choices.text: 7 flaky, 13 passed
choices.why: Flaky needs retries and an attempt that failed first; there were no retries.

prompt: Which of these should a quarantined test carry?

choices.text: An owner
choices.why: Right. Somebody is responsible for bringing it back.

choices.text: A date to look at it again
choices.why: Right. Without one, a quarantine is a deletion done slowly.

choices.text: The reason, and what must be true for it to return
choices.why: Right. The comment above the test says what the defect is and when it goes back into `tests/`.

choices.text: A higher number of retries
choices.why: Retries keep a test in the gate and hide it; a quarantine takes it out and counts it.

choices.text: A `test.skip()` so it stops failing
choices.why: A skipped test stops looking; the quarantine job exists so it keeps running.

prompt: Why would raising the timeout of the typing test's last check not fix it?

choices.text: The timeout is ignored with `--repeat-each`
choices.why: Each attempt has its timeout; the failing attempt took 6.1 s because it waited out five seconds.

choices.text: The final list is wrong, and more waiting changes nothing about it
choices.why: Right. A limit of thirty seconds would make the failure take thirty seconds and fail the same way.

choices.text: The server answers too fast for a longer wait to matter
choices.why: Speed is not the issue; the answers arrive, in an order that leaves the wrong list.

choices.text: Playwright caps a check's timeout at five seconds
choices.why: Five seconds is the default, and it can be raised; raising it is the wrong fix, not an impossible one.

prompt: After the search fix, the quarantine job passes 20 of 20. Before it, the test failed 5, 6 and 8 attempts in twenty. How strong is that evidence?

choices.text: Weak: twenty passes prove nothing about a flaky test
choices.why: That holds for a rare failure; at one in four, twenty passes by luck are about 3 in 1,000.

choices.text: Strong: by luck that streak would happen about 3 times in 1,000
choices.why: Right. 0.75 raised to the power 20 is about 0.003, and the fix can also be explained from the code.

choices.text: Complete: the defect cannot come back
choices.why: No count proves a future; a later change to `search.js` can bring the race back, which is why the test stays.

choices.text: Unknown until the run is repeated with `--retries 2`
choices.why: Retries can only turn failures into flaky passes; they make a green streak weaker evidence, not stronger.

prompt: A test truly fails one attempt in twenty. In what percentage of runs of twenty attempts would all twenty pass anyway? Round to a whole number.
hint: Each attempt passes with probability 0.95, and the twenty are independent.

prompt: A test that checks a date printed on the order page fails on CI, which runs in UTC, from 21:00 to midnight São Paulo time, and passes on every laptop in the team. Which cause fits, and what is the fix?

choices.text: Timing; wait for the date to appear
choices.why: The date appears; it is a different day in UTC for those three hours, and waiting will not change the day.

choices.text: Shared state; reset the shop before the test
choices.why: Nothing another test writes explains a failure tied to the clock and the machine's time zone.

choices.text: The application; quarantine the test until the page is fixed
choices.why: The page may be right for the zone it was asked in; first find whether the test or the machine assumed a zone.

choices.text: Environment; fix zone and clock
choices.why: Right. Remove the difference between machines: the test sets the zone and the time it means, as Playwright's `timezoneId` and a fixed clock allow.
